prompt.en: A two-metre station logs a 950 km contact during a calm evening with a sharp temperature change above the ground. Which explanation best fits the unusual range?

text.en: Ordinary VHF line-of-sight with no atmospheric help
Tropospheric ducting caused by a temperature inversion
Faraday rotation making the path shorter

explanation.en: The distance is beyond the normal VHF planning scale, and the stable temperature layering is a classic clue for ducting in the lower atmosphere.

prompt.en: During a short early-summer opening, a six-metre station hears many stations from one distant region while two metres stays local. Which cause is most plausible?

text.en: Lower-HF ground wave extending to VHF
A temporary E-layer opening affecting low VHF
Tropospheric scatter becoming strongest only on HF

explanation.en: Six metres is the VHF band most associated with sporadic-E style openings. A short regional opening on six but not two metres points toward an E-layer event.

prompt.en: A permanent UHF service link just beyond the radio horizon is weak but usable without a weather duct. Which mode should the engineer consider?

text.en: Tropospheric scatter from small lower-atmosphere variations
Meteor scatter with continuous hour-long reflections
Sporadic E as a guaranteed daily VHF layer
Ground wave as the dominant UHF long-distance path

explanation.en: Tropospheric scatter can support weak beyond-horizon VHF/UHF paths by redirecting a small part of the signal in the lower atmosphere, even without a well-formed duct.
